entries.title: The 24 Very Best Amazon Black Friday Deals to Get Now (2026)
entries.summary: For die-hard Amazon shoppers, the retailer’s “Black Friday Week” sale is now live. Grab these deals on our favorite (and tested) products through November 30.
entries.content:
Amazon’s Black Friday deals are a go. Its “Black Friday Week” sale runs from now until November 30 (Cyber Monday), giving shoppers a head start on holiday shopping. To help you sift through the many products, we’ve highlighted some of our favorites below. If you’re a big Amazon shopper, now is a great time to fill those holiday wish lists and spend Black Friday with friends and family.

Check out our guide to the best Early Black Friday deals, plus standing desk deals, Home Depot appliance savings, and early tech deals.

Updated November 24: We’ve updated this story with more deals on products we’ve tested and recommend.

Jump To

Best Amazon Black Friday Tech Deals

When Apple raised prices earlier this year, the once-affordable MacBook Air now starts at $1,300. The MacBook Air is still the best Apple laptop for most people, even some pro users, thanks to the M5 chipset’s power and efficiency. This Black Friday deal brings the 13-inch base model below $1,000, the price it used to be before the increase. Its 15-inch sibling is also on sale for $1,199, down from $1,499.

The Arc Ultra is a soundbar that does it right, delivering great all-around performance from a single speaker. Our current pick as the best soundbar you can buy, the Arc Ultra supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X surround sound to create cinema-quality audio in your living room. For a true surround setup, the Sonos Ultimate Immersive Set with Arc Ultra is also on sale and includes a subwoofer and two additional speakers.

The best iPad for most people isn’t one of Apple’s more powerful options, which says a lot. The base iPad runs on the older A16 chipset, but it can handle most of what people use a tablet for: streaming entertainment, web browsing, email, drawing, and even light productivity work. It’s great for casual users, including kids. This Black Friday deal brings the price closer to its previous MSRP, before Apple’s price increase. Check out more Black Friday iPad Deals.

While you can often find this router at this sale price, it’s still a deal for the best budget Wi-Fi router for a small home. It’s not the most powerful router, and it doesn’t support the 6 GHz band, but if your needs are basic, it will more than suffice.

With a WIRED rating of 9 out of 10, the XM6 is one of our favorite over-ear headphones, combining comfort with great sound quality and noise cancellation. This is the lowest price on Amazon; however, it has dropped to this price before. Note that Walmart and Best Buy are also offering the XM6 at this sale price.

Good gaming laptops are never cheap, and they’ve become even more expensive this year. If you need a recommendation that balances performance and budget, we recommend the Asus ROG Strix G16 with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060, one of our favorite budget gaming laptops. We prefer the RTX 5070 option, but it’s nearly $3,000. This on-sale model is more attainable.

The latest Echo Show 11 is our recommendation for the Best Alexa Smart Display. WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell found the screen bright and crisp, with immersive sound quality. Since the sale price matches the regular price of the smaller Echo Show 8, it’s a good deal—just $5 more than the sale price during Amazon’s October Prime Day event.

The Pixel 11-series phones from Google are among our favorite Android devices. Loaded with the latest software and Gemini AI features, the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro XL are our pick as the smartest Android smartphones. They’re also the only non-iPhones to support Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic mounting, so you can use MagSafe accessories. During Black Friday, you can get all for under $1,000 each—a terrific deal for a flagship phone—and they’re at their lowest price ever on Amazon.

High-quality three-in-one charging stands look terrific on a bedside table, but many cost over $100. This one from Mophie is one of our favorites, and it’s 49 percent off on Amazon right now.

The AirTag seems to be on sale all the time, but no matter—it’s currently the lowest price on Amazon and cheaper than buying from Apple. It’s one of the best Bluetooth trackers. If you can swing it, go for the four-pack.

Alongside the AirTag, the AirPods Max 2 and AirPods Pro 3 are also on sale. These are well-regarded among WIRED testers, but we recommend waiting until after Thanksgiving to see if they drop further—don’t worry, they are often on sale.

Phone accessories are aplenty on Amazon, but few look as good as Moft’s. You can pick up this ingenious wallet-kickstand hybrid that attaches to an iPhone via MagSafe, or peruse the rest of Moft's Black Friday deals.

You can expect Amazon’s own devices to go on sale during Black Friday. While Blink’s security cameras didn’t make our short list, WIRED reviewer Simon Hill still thinks they’re worth considering, especially if you’re on a budget. A downer is that they only work with Alexa, but if that’s your smart home setup, it’s NBD. The latest version of its pan-tilt camera is usually $50, but it’s 60 percent off right now.

WIRED’s audio editor won’t stop praising Soundcore products, but he’s not wrong: This nascent brand (soon to be rebranded as Anker, its parent company) makes terrific audio products without the premium price. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe included this Bluetooth boom box in a roundup of her favorite festival gear. It’s the lowest price ever on Amazon currently, but it’s not the cheapest—keep an eye out at other retailers during Black Friday.

This EcoFlow portable battery is WIRED reviewer Simon Hill’s pick as the best power bank for laptops. It has a large 27,650-mAh capacity, which is plenty for charging smaller devices too. It’s great for travel since it’s allowed on a plane, and it has a retractable USB-C cable, so you can leave extras at home.

At $359, the second-gen Bose QuietComfort over-ear headphones seem overpriced considering the competition. But when they’re on sale at $199 to $219 (depending on the color), they suddenly become a great buy. As expected from Bose, the noise cancellation and sound quality are excellent. They are also comfortable, making them great travel companions. Note that the first-gen version is also on sale for $169 (it’s frequently at this price), but it’s outdated, and we think you should spend $30 to $50 more on the latest version instead.

Amazon Early Black Friday Home and Kitchen Deals

Gone are the days of putting up holiday lights and then taking them down, only to do it again the next year. These outdoor lights are designed to stay up permanently; when they’re not displaying colorful holiday lights, they can shine white for regular everyday lighting. They work with any smart home platform, so you can control them via an app or a voice assistant.

WIRED Reviews Editor Kat Merck is our resident bird expert, having tested numerous bird feeders and doing extensive research on her feathered friends who visit her home. One of the best bird feeders she’s used is on sale at Amazon at the lowest price ever. The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is easy to clean and has a solar roof for wire-free camera charging. The app even has a handy bird-identification feature to help you determine what species stopped by.

It seems like every appliance maker offers an air fryer, but if you want the best, the Typhur Dome 2 should be at the top of your shortlist. It’s also on sale this Black Friday, which makes this “splurge” item a bit easier on the holiday budget. Our reviewer found it works fast during testing, and it can bake as well as cook a pizza or steak.

As a premium home appliance maker, Dyson doesn’t make cheap products. Which is why Black Friday is a good time to see what might go on sale. Right now, our top pick for the most affordable Dyson vacuum cleaner is even cheaper—the lowest price we’ve seen yet. It works on both hard and carpeted floors, and its brush system can handle all sorts of debris.

Love them or hate them, but pod-based coffee makers are popular for their convenience. The Nespresso Vertuo Pop+ is our recommended espresso pod maker, and the Deluxe model is under $100. It has a larger water tank than the standard version, and the Vertuo pods are recyclable. For more savings on coffee-related products, check out our Early Black Friday Espresso Machine Deals.

WIRED’s home-cleaning expert, Nena Farrell, recommended only three robot vacuums, naming this Eufy floor-sweeping automaton her budget pick. It’s 53 percent off right now—the lowest price ever on Amazon—for a robovac with great suction power and a self-cleaning roller mop.

With quality espresso machines costing $500 and more (way, way more), a budget option seems improbable. Yet, this De’Longhi fits the bill. One of our recommended models, it usually costs around $200 or just a little more, but you can snag one for $150 if you’ve been wanting to get into the third-wave coffee game. It’s a great price, but we’ve seen it go as low as $120 in past sales.

entries.title: Best Black Friday Nintendo Switch 2 Deals (2026): Bundles, Games
entries.summary: Get your game on for less with these Black Friday deals on official Nintendo Switch 2 bundles and games.
entries.content:
While video games generally drop in price quickly, Nintendo is a bit of an exception to the rule—it rarely discounts its first-party titles. But I've spotted a few Black Friday deals on official Nintendo Switch 2 bundles, Nintendo Switch 2 games, and original Switch games. These deals are live on the official Nintendo Store, but you can also expect to find them at all major retailers.

Sadly, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is not on the list, but here’s what is on offer. (We'll add more Nintendo deals to this list as they pop up.)

Best Black Friday Nintendo Switch 2 Deals

The original and best Nintendo Switch 2 bundle is this one, combining a Nintendo Switch 2 console, a full download of the Mario Kart World game, and a 3-Month (90-Day) Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership.

The ultimate party game, Mario Kart World offers open-world racing chaos with a huge cast of characters. Whether you play split-screen or go for online multiplayer battles against up to 23 other players, this title offers the greatest replayability and fun of any Nintendo Switch 2 game. This bundle costs $500, which is a decent $50 saving.

If you want something a little different, this is the other Switch 2 bundle that’s on sale. Once again, you get a Nintendo Switch 2 system and three months of Nintendo Switch Online Individual Membership, but this time it’s paired with the Nintendo Switch Sports Resort game.

This title includes all your old Wii Sports favorites (Tennis, Golf, Bowling, and Boxing), everything from Wii Sports Resort (Archery, Basketball, Table Tennis, Power Cruising, and Prop Plane), and three new options (Volleyball, Skateboarding, and Thumb Wrestling). This bundle is available for $530, which is around $28 off the usual price.

Best Black Friday Nintendo Switch Game Deals

There are several deals on Switch 2 games at $20 off the usual price, so Black Friday is a good time to fill out your library before the holidays. These titles are all available as downloads from the Nintendo Store, but you should find the same discounts on physical copies from all the major retailers:

  • Donkey Kong Bananza for $50 ($20 off)
  • Kirby Air Riders for $50 ($20 off)
  • Metroid Prime 4: Beyond – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition for $50 ($20 off)
  • Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2 for $50 ($20 off)
  • Super Mario Party Jamboree – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Jamboree TV for $60 ($20 off)

These discounts also apply to the original Switch versions of Metroid Prime 4: Beyond and Super Mario Party Jamboree .

There are also even bigger discounts on several third-party Nintendo Switch 2 games, such as:

  • Sonic X Shadow Generations for $20 ($30 off)
  • Star Wars Outlaws for $15 ($45 off)

entries.title: Anthropic Created a Honeypot to Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving
entries.summary: A new test assumes AI agents can go rogue—and asks whether they can resist temptation.
entries.content:
Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots.

Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures.

The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sit just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that’s cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps.

“Models are going to continue getting better, continue finding zero-day vulnerabilities,” says Darya Kaviani, a researcher at Anthropic who specializes in security and helped develop Siren.

A zero-day vulnerability is a previously unknown flaw in a piece of software that can be used to pilfer data or gain unauthorized access. Anthropic’s Mythos models are especially skilled at finding zero day bugs because they lack the guardrails that normally block this kind of potentially malicious activity.

Kaviani says we should assume AI models will become increasingly capable of finding and exploiting zero-days, or figuring out other ways to break free from their constraints. The question then becomes whether they’ll resist the temptation to do so.

AI agents—models that perfect actions autonomously—are becoming increasingly commonplace. They power capable coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, as well as peppy personal assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots.

But the rise of helpful agents has been accompanied by some remarkable bad behavior. Agents tested by Anthropic, OpenAI, and others have broken free from sandboxes and even hacked into other companies in an effort to solve challenging problems.

Assuming AI models continue to display such ingenuity, Kaviani says it will be crucial to do more than just patch software. “Even as we strengthen our infrastructure, models will be able to also keep up and be able to find vulnerabilities,” Kaviani says.

Earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks.

“We’ve added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments,” says Oscar O’Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. “This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much.”

O’Rahilly says that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also showed that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free.

In Anthropic’s tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively.

AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they’re being tested. But O’Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test.

As AI models get ever-smarter, many researchers worry about whether they’ll outwit their human counterparts. If that does happen, then it may be essential that agents—and not just the executives responsible for them—can resist temptation.

entries.title: Thanksgiving Travel Will Be a Stormy Mess
entries.summary: Snow, wind, rain, flooding. Storms on both coasts mean the holiday travel week will have it all—and it could wreak havoc at airports across the US.
entries.content:
Expect travel headaches from coast to coast this week. Several rounds of disruptive weather sweep are likely to cause delays at airports and make for challenging driving conditions just in time for the Thanksgiving long weekend.

A very active pattern draped across North America will keep the storm train running in the days ahead. Potent systems rolling into the West Coast will bring disruptions from Seattle to San Francisco, where high tides could swamp airport runways. East of the Rockies, a major coastal storm expected to develop on Wednesday will generate widespread heavy rain and winds so gusty there’s a “significant chance” the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade could be balloonless for the first time in 55 years. The same system will also deliver the season’s first measurable snow in some areas.

The stormy setup arrives at the peak travel time of the year in the US. The Transportation Security Administration screened 3.1 million passengers to close out the long weekend in 2025, marking the agency’s highest passenger volume on record. And with the extreme weather this week is set to sweep across some of the country’s biggest travel hubs, it could upend the best-laid travel plans.

West Coast Storms

A persistent series of low-pressure systems will drag waves of heavy precipitation into the Pacific Northwest throughout the week, making delays and the occasional cancellation likely for flyers in Seattle and Portland.

The real risk for delays begins to pile up when rain and gusty winds follow a cold front into northern California on Tuesday night Though the worst of the rain will likely clear out in time for the bulk of Wednesday’s travel, flooding is still a major concern for low-lying highways and parts of San Francisco International Airport.

Forecasters expect a near-record king tide—that is, one of the highest tides of the year—on Tuesday and Wednesday. King tides are a normal occurrence, but this year’s will be exacerbated by record-high sea levels driven by the Super El Niño. The climate phenomenon has pushed warm water toward the coast, which takes up more space than cold water.

Monday’s forecast from the National Weather Service called for a high tide of 8.5 feet at the San Francisco gauge on Wednesday morning, which is just shy of the all-time record of 8.66 feet set in January 1983, another Super El Niño year.

East Coast Nor’easter Risk

Farther east, the atmospheric ingredients are lining up for a sprawling nor’easter to develop over the Southeast by Wednesday and move north through New England by the end of the week.

Widespread heavy rainfall will accompany the storm northward, potentially worsening highway traffic as commuters and vacationers alike navigate slick roads in gloomy conditions. Gusty winds will reduce visibility during heavy rainfall. Forecasters expect several inches of rain along the East Coast, especially along the Interstate 95 corridor between South Carolina and New York.

Airline delays are almost certain given the dreaded mix of precipitation, low clouds, and stiff winds. The greatest impacts are likely in Charlotte and Raleigh in North Carolina on Wednesday, followed by Washington, DC, Philadelphia, New York, and Boston on Thursday.

All these cities are home to major hubs for various airlines. Foul conditions at one of those airports can have ripple effects that lead to delayed or canceled flights down the line, including in cities where the weather is just fine. This may be the most impactful Thanksgiving weather since a nor’easter rolled up the East Coast on the Wednesday and Thursday of the holiday weekend in 2014. That storm hit the major hubs with high winds and heavy rain, as well as up to a foot of wet snow across much of the interior Northeast. The event led to thousands of cancelled and delayed flights. (The US also got a taste of travel trouble earlier this month when a Federal Aviation Administration ground stop left travelers stranded.)

The conditions could get so dire, that the Macy’s parade could go on but sans balloons. The parade will ground its balloons if there are sustained winds of 24 mph or gusts of 35 mph. The National Weather Service issued a high wind watch for New York City beginning Thursday morning, with winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 60 mph possible, though when the nor’easter reaches New York will determine if the winds cross that crucial threshold during the parade.

Cold air wrapping into the western side of the same storm system could lead to the first measurable snow of the season throughout portions of the Midwest. Computer models are still a bit wishy-washy on exactly where and how much snow will fall, as the rain-snow line will depend on the precise track of the storm. As of Monday, the general consensus for a few inches of wet snow appears to focus on the St. Louis metro area east into central Illinois.

There’s some good news for travelers in the eastern US, at least: The nor’easter is expected to clear out by Saturday morning, which should hopefully reduce any snarls for travelers headed home on Sunday.

entries.title: 8 Best Espresso Machines for Home (2026), Tested by Coffee Pros
entries.summary: The best espresso makers can turn your kitchen into a café and help you hone the art of the perfect shot.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

The Best espresso machines for home must thread a delicate needle. Espresso is forceful and finicky, and a little intimidating, and yet so essential that astronauts might take it into orbit. A home espresso machine remains the most intense and expensive device I regularly operate before my first cup of coffee.

I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don’t make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup. And so my top-rated espresso machine, the Fellow Series 1, earned its place on WIRED’s counter by combining ease of use with a solid build, consistent temperature, and rare control over pressure—an industry-beating mix of nerdiness and hand-holding friendliness. For a more classic, all-analog build, we offer the compact, stylish Diletta Mio.

But I know not everyone wants to also buy a good coffee grinder or spend four figures for their morning cup. For those who want milk-based drinks and a built-in grinder, I recommend the top-selling Breville Barista Express as the Goldilocks machine balancing performance and cost. For an entry-level device, I pretty much always recommend the straight-ahead Breville Bambino, among the lowest-cost machines with PID-controlled temperature.

Note that this guide mostly covers classic, hands-on espresso machines with portafilters. We do also include the De'Longhi Rivelia, our top pick among super-automatic espresso machines that require little more than a button press. For a guide that focuses on easy-to-use espresso machine picks that do most of the work for you, check out our guide to the Best Latte and Automatic Espresso Machines.

Also, be sure to check out our other coffee guides, like the Best Drip Coffee Makers, Best Cold Brew Makers, Best Aeropresses, Best Coffee Pod Machines, Best Coffee Subscriptions, and Best Coffee Grinders.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on Meraki’s second-run release and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Compare the Top 8 Espresso Machines

Fellow Series 1 Semiautomatic, touchscreen None Y $1500 2+ years

De'Longhi Classic Classic (pressurized basket) Nope Y $230 1 year
Flair Signature Espresso Maker Manual None N $229 3 years

Frequently Asked Questions

How Do I Test Espresso Machines?

Over the past decade, WIRED has tested dozens of espresso makers to find our favorites. The process, in part, is simple. We brew a whole lot of coffee. I’ve written about coffee for more than a decade on both the East and West Coasts, including my hometown coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon. Other current and past WIRED espresso testers—who include former baristas and longtime coffee writers—include Jaina Grey, Jeffrey Van Camp, Kat Merck, Tyler Shane, Pete Cottell, and Scott Gilbertson.

On each machine that’s capable, I make and assess at least four styles of drink, on multiple roasts and beans: a basic 2:1 espresso, an Americano, a latte, and a cappuccino. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts.

I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it, and on any of my top picks I've made at least fifty drinks. Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner—and so some of our less-recommended devices are dismissed a bit earlier.

What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. But also, I’m looking for ease, the thoughtful touches that make an espresso maker something you can fall in love with.

I test whether the hot water spout splatters, whether descaling requires a degree in hydrology, whether the brewing temperature is consistent, and whether the latte milk gets silked. I’m truly terrible at latte art, but whether it’s possible is a straightforward test of the body of the frothed milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk.

On machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent.

On any semiautomatic machine that decides the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you're getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again.

I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood.

How I Select Espresso Machines to Review

In part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De'Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade shows, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations.

I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most users. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest.

But I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you.

This means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal.

The lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino.

But hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better.

What Beans Are Best for Espresso?

First off, there's no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it says on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso.

But traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that's often what they mean.

Does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries.

It's up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you'll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. (See here for an explainer on light-roast espresso.) But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans.

One thing that's true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They'll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they've begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are more likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors.

Obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you'll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can't find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they're not fresh. And your espresso will be worse. For fresh beans delivered to your house, check out WIRED's guide to the best coffee subscriptions.

Espresso Accessories That Make for Great Cups

If you're spending this much on an espresso machine, you'll want to invest in a good grinder and even a scale, as well as a few other devices that make your shots better, and your life a little easier.

An espresso-capable grinder: If your espresso machine doesn't come with a grinder, you'll need one. Preground bag beans are especially difficult to use when making espresso, and will likely lead to off-flavors or channeling. But not just any grinder will do. You'll need a good grinder that can grind consistent beans finely enough for espresso. WIRED's top-pick Baratza Encore ESP is always a good choice—positioned squarely at the fulcrum where more expensive grinders begin to offer diminishing returns.

An accurate scale with a timer: Most grinders, and a goodly portion of espresso machines, do not offer a precise scale. But a precise scale is what you need to get espresso ratios right. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu loved the Acaia brew-by-weight scale ($400) that automatically connects to the La Marzocco Linea Mini and a few other devices via its companion app. But a far less sophisticated scale can still help you measure your shot size and control the dose you want on each espresso shot. If you're not precious about beauty, there's always this low-cost, little no-name scale. It's accurate to a 10th of a gram, and has a timer to boot.

The best knockbox: When you're done with that portafilter filled with coffee grounds, what do you do with it? Beat it against the side of a trashcan? Dig out those grounds into the sink? Nah. You need a good knock box. And somehow this jobby-job from Breville is the best one I've ever found. It's sturdy, the cross bar is in the right spot so that the grinds dump cleanly into the bin, and the bottom has enough grip that the box doesn't scoot around on the counter. Simplicity is competence.

Not all steaming pitchers are created equal, notes WIRED contributing reviewer (and former barista) Pete Cottell. As opposed to the sad piece of aluminum that probably came with your espresso maker, this Brewista offers thick walls for heat retention, a precision tip for expert latte pours, and a thermometer sticker on its side so you can get a rough gauge of milk temperature without hunting down an actual thermometer. It can also take a beating. This is your new frothing pitcher.

Other Machines We Like

Breville Oracle Jet for $2,000: The Breville Oracle Jet is my previous top pick for threading that delicate needle between ease and deliciousness, before getting displaced by my new top-pick Fellow device. The Oracle Jet remains a powerful and frankly beautiful stainless-steel machine, with sterling temperature control and a solid built-in grinder that uses the same conical burrs as the excellent Baratza Encore ESP ($200). This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from an Americano to a flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini. And yet the Jet's easily accessible for anyone who can figure out an iPhone, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You'll be nose-deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. Note that manual milk steaming with the Jet's powerful wand is still better than the automatic version.

Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro for $750: Tradition is the opposite of what Ninja does. This is the company that made the soft-serve Swirl, the Slushi, and the portable air fryer. Ninja is all about the extras. And Ninja doesn't judge. And so of course Ninja jumped in with both feet on cold-foam coldspresso. In fact, the new Luxe Cafe Pro makes the best cold foam out of any espresso machine I've tried, with a whisk that whips up plant milk or cow milk into thick, creamy, dense, beautiful froth—ready for your ridiculously complicated cold caramel-vanilla latte TikTok recipe. What I didn't expect was that Ninja would also nail the fundamentals so well, on only its second entry into the espresso market. The relatively accurate by-weight dosing is nice. So is the excellent steam wand that also outpaces most contenders on automatic hot foaming, adjustable to multiple densities of foam. The Pro clears up some oversights in the previous-model Premier, including an easy tamping lever, and a hot water spout. Maintenance, whether descaling or purging, is also as easy as it gets. Just don't use this grinder with light roast beans. Medium or dark only.

Breville Oracle Dual Boiler for $3,000: This update to the previous Breville Dual Boiler espresso machine is a powerful, truly impressive machine in many regards. It combines the easy touchscreen operation and automatic dosing and tamping of WIRED's previous top-pick Oracle Jet with a welcome “manual” mode that lets you play with pre-infusion and bloom while monitoring a digital pressure gauge on the touchscreen. I kinda love this as an exercise in future-retro design—or whatever the inverse of steampunk is—but also as a means of really controlling my shot, and getting a lot more crema and body out of it. The dual boiler heats up very fast—like four minutes fast—and gives you the wonderful temperature stability and consistency you expect from a dual boiler, plus the ability to steam milk and make espresso simultaneously. The production model I received had a very tight portafilter fit, which loosened up after the first 30 shots or so but initially required some muscle. I also haven't been able to get good results with lighter-roast beans, which led to the occasional under-filled portafilter that had to be retamped manually. We'll update as we resolve those quirks, but can attest that for medium to dark beans, this Dual Boiler is an absolute beast.

Meraki Espresso Machine for $1,999: When former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage first tested this high-design “steampunk gasworks” of an espresso machine, he loved the features for the price, including a Timemore grinder that grinds by weight, PID temperature control, easy pre-infusion, and another scale under the brewer that lets you control output. He did not, however, love having to overrotate the portafilter for a proper fit, or the wackily complicated descaling procedure. I’ve since tested the second run of this machine (the one you’ll be getting if you buy right now) and did not have any trouble with the portafilter. You’ll also get 45 grind settings instead of the original 30, though we were hard-pressed to discern a real difference from the additional 15. —Kat Merck

Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier for $600: Ninja has already released an upgraded Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro version ($750) after its espresso machine debut. But its first device, the Luxe Cafe Premier, is already a corker, a low-priced all-in-one with cold brew, coffee, espresso, excellent milk frothing, and unexpected luxury features like a built-in scale so the grinder can dose by weight. The device can feel either overstuffed or generous, depending on who you are. Either way, this damn near unseated the Breville Barista Express as WIRED’s mid-tier top pick, aside from a few leaks and sensible caution about its durability.

De'Longhi La Specialista Opera for $800: Speaking of espresso makers that came running at Breville, this Opera is a beautifully forgiving semiautomatic machine that makes excellent espresso in the medium- to dark-roast range, with non-pressurized portafilter baskets that make for a nice and surprisingly subtle cup. It’s the best De'Longhi espresso machine I’ve tested, in many ways, among the semiautomatic camp. The Opera sports a lot of options—including dose and temperature control—while remaining refreshingly analog with its satisfying metal frame, metal buttons, and prominent pressure gauge. Cold brew is a perk for those who like milk. The grinder is decent, though its 15 settings might not offer enough sensitivity to pull the best from each roast. One could wish for a removable hopper and a sturdier tamping lever. But if you or your partner love cold coffee drinks or espresso martinis, this gives comparable Brevilles a strong run for the money.

De'Longhi La Specialista Touch for $800: De'Longhi’s new Touch, released this year, isn't merely a touchscreen version of the very analog Opera—though it is just as handsome as the Opera. Instead, it offers a very specific set of trade-offs. Like De'Longhi's Rivelia, there's a bean-assist function that you can save for each bean you like. It also has a better steam wand, with the ability to read the temperature of the milk you're steaming as you steam it. In fact, it's maybe more intuitive overall. But it doesn't quite offer the easy customization on temperature, shot time, or ratios. The cold brew is not quite as well-dialed as the Opera. The Touch is an Italian machine on training wheels, designed for Italian-style medium to dark shots. This should work for most people, but minus a pressure bar or a shot timer, it can also feel like a bit of a black box.

La Marzocco Linea Mini for $6,600: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu spent two weeks with La Marzocco's Linea Mini, a home version of the fancy espresso machines you'll see in coffee shops around the world. The price may be eye-searing, but Chokkattu did find the resulting elixir to be absolutely fantastic—and the same went for La Marzocco's customer service while Chokkattu was dialing in his machine. It offers a lot of room for experimentation, and it sports a killer cool-touch steam wand that froths milk in seconds.

De'Longhi Stilosa for $150: The Stilosa was our top budget pick for years. It's still a good budget pick, and it often goes on sale for less than $100. You're not going to get high-end features like a pressure gauge or built-in grinder, and it's a little plasticky. But what the Stilosa does provide is everything you need to make great espresso at home: a solid portafilter, a reliable steam pump, and a steaming wand. It is a little light, so you'll want to brace it when you mount and dismount the portafilter (or it might slide around on you). After brewing cup after cup of espresso, the Stilosa never showed signs of slowing or breaking down the way many inexpensive machines can. In fact, we're now revisiting the Stilosa as our budget pick, after catching a few tips on how to use the Stilosa for light roast espresso.

Breville Barista Express Impress for $800: This espresso machine is the more tricked-out sibling of the Breville Barista Express. It includes more grind and dosing settings and automates some of the more complicated parts of brewing consistently good espresso, like getting just the right amount of beans ground per shot.

Breville Dual Boiler for $1,600: The previous-generation Breville Dual Boiler is an absolute tank of an espresso machine. It's huge. It's heavy. It makes amazing espresso. But while its size makes brewing espresso feel luxurious, it does eat up a lot of space and needs a little time to heat up, versus newer Brevilles like the Oracle Jet that favor thermoblock-style heaters. But a dual boiler does mean you can brew shot after shot, with steamed milk and hot water at the same time, without having to wait in between shots. The new Breville Oracle Dual Boiler ($3,000) is already on the market, but you can still pick up the previous generation for half the price.

Cuisinart EM-160 Slim for $250: The lowest-cost espresso maker from Cuisinart's new espresso line is among the slimmer espresso machines out there, less than 7 inches across. This makes it a treasure for certain kitchens. The espresso quality is about what you'd expect from a pressurized portafilter: smoother, less nuanced, but also pretty forgiving for beginners trying to dial in a bean. This'll be best for those who mix milk with their espresso. Same goes for the fast-dripped “cold espresso” option, which takes a couple minutes to complete and comes out a bit tannic, but mixes well with cold milk or a lot of ice. You'll need a grinder if you don't want sad supermarket beans.

Superkop Manual Espresso Maker for $800: This manual espresso machine is technically not a Jackie Chan movie. The Superkop is instead a quite finely engineered espresso device. It looks pretty, and unlike other manual espresso machines, you don't need a strong arm to use it. So if you want to pull espresso, but not pull it hard, the Superkop is your huckleberry. That said, $600 is a lot of money for a manual device. Buy it if you know you'll love it.

Also Tried

Gevi Espresso Machine With Grinder and Milk Frother for $350: WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell prized the pressure control and built-in grinder on this Gevi espresso machine, when you take into account the near-unfathomable low price for a machine with this functionality. Alas, a somewhat erratic steam wand makes it hard to recommend.

Cuisinart EM-640 Espresso Bar for $650: Cuisinart rolled in with some ambition on this semiautomatic espresso machine, with a built-in grinder and a non-pressurized, bottomless portafilter meant to play in the same sandbox as Breville's top devices. Alas, I really couldn't get consistency on either dosing or grinding from the device's built-in grinder—and the system for customizing the dose in particular was mostly wild guesswork. This all added up to botched shots, wild spray from the portafilter, and none of the ease one wants from a semiautomatic.

De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $700: This semiautomatic De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo comes with a built-in burr grinder and makes great espresso right out of the box, and is slimmer than other espresso machines in its category. It does have quirks: It includes a little plastic adapter needed to attach the portafilter to the grinder spout, and a little stepstool for your espresso cup to keep the coffee from splashing. It’s a good machine, but I'd upgrade to the Opera any day of the week.

entries.title: Gift Ideas for Friends (2026): Wellness Tech, Kitchen Essentials
entries.summary: These are the WIRED-tested gadgets, kitchen tools, and cozy comforts I’d actually buy for my own inner circle.
entries.content:
In writing this guide on gift ideas for friends, I learned that there really is no catchall gift that will please everyone. Choosing these gifts, I thought back to some of the best self-care products and tech I’ve tested recently. I included the gadgets I reach for regularly, as well as those I’ve bought for family and friends after testing and loving them. So please use this guide as a starting point, keeping your friend’s personality, needs, and hobbies in mind as you shop for the right gifts.

After testing hundreds of products during my years on the WIRED Reviews team, these are the items I’d recommend to the friends on my own list. I’ve included self-care gifts like massagers, cozy gifts like an ultrasoft throw blanket, kitchen staples like a chef’s knife, and everything in between. There are many gifts at different price points, and they’re also categorized by gift type below. Be sure to check back often, as I will be updating this guide with versatile new picks as we get closer to gifting season.

Looking for more gift ideas? Don’t miss our other awesome gift guides as the holiday season ramps up.

Updated November 24: I’ve updated links and prices and added more gifts from Sonos, HexClad, Owala, Grace & Stella, Ursa Major, Ole Henrickson, Lndn Gray, Lenox, Gumball Poodle, Galison, Brass Monkey, Tocca, WineWhiz, Nimble, and Belkin.

Best Tech Gifts

It’s my belief that everyone could use a small, portable Bluetooth speaker. Whether you want to sing along to your tunes in the shower or get the party going around a campfire, having a compact, Bluetooth-enabled speaker at the ready makes you everyone’s favorite party guest. At less than $60, I promise this li’l guy will be a hit as a gift (without breaking the bank). Plus, you can fully customize the design with images, text, and stickers if you want to make it more personalized for the giftee.

If your friend wants a great home speaker for sound (not voice assistant tasks), the Sonos Era 100 SL is an excellent, microphone-free option. It is a huge step up in terms of sound quality—it can easily fill any smaller room (think apartment living) with rich, detailed instrumentation. And if they decide they love it, they can easily pair it with other Sonos speakers. —Harry Rabinowitz

Best Self-Care Gifts

This nifty gadget from wellness tech company Chirp is a godsend for anyone who’s always on their feet. It has two sides: One features a textured surface that targets pressure points, and the other has a heated, centralized oval that acts like a hot stone for targeted arch relief. The end has a USB-C charging port and buttons to adjust heat, vibration, and preset recovery programs, which use different heat and massage patterns for relief. I use this gadget almost daily, especially if I’ve been on my feet a lot that day. This is the perfect gift for someone who’s always asking for a foot massage.

This surprisingly affordable skin care box set is the perfect gift for a friend who loves facial products or could use a little self-care. It includes a hydrating serum, energizing gold eye masks, a face mask, rose spray, face balm, and lip mask. Its focus on hydration is especially ideal for the dry winter months.

Best Cozy Gifts

WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane was sold on Hatch’s newest sunrise alarm clock, which also doubles as a sleep tracker. If your giftee doesn’t want to sleep with a wearable to get their sleep stats, this device uses motion-based tracking to provide passive sleep monitoring from their nightstand. It functions as a sunrise clock, a dimmable bedside light, and a sound machine, and it now captures data like sleep duration and stages, presented in interactive visuals. Boutayna loved the refreshing minimalist design, with no cameras or microphones watching you sleep. Best of all, your data is not locked behind a Hatch+ membership. If you have a friend who struggles with sleep or waking up, consider joining in the sunrise alarm clock trend and getting them this aesthetic bedside machine.

Best Kitchen Gifts

Everyone—I mean every single person—needs at least one great chef’s knife. This is probably the most important multipurpose kitchen tool—it can slice, dice, and chop ingredients with speed and precision. Your friend most likely could use a better knife for everyday cooking. Great chefs’ knives range from less than $100 to several hundred dollars, but I really like this mid-range, 8-inch knife from Material. It’s made from luxe Japanese high-carbon stainless steel for extra durability, with a matte, stain-resistant composite handle. Plus, if you buy from Material’s site, you can add an engraved message for a fun, more personal touch.

If your friend is a wine enthusiast, or you want to impress at the next dinner party, I love these easy-to-use, accessible wine opener sets. This set includes an electric opener and aerator, plus a carrying case. WineWhiz also has its flagship ready-to-wrap box set, which I tested and liked, that makes a great gift and includes a foil cutter and vacuum sealer. But I love the idea of bringing a great bottle of wine and a fancy new opener with a cute carrying case to your holiday party and gifting both.

entries.title: This Hollywood Star Took on Crypto. Now He’s Got a New Target
entries.summary: Ben McKenzie is launching a nonprofit to take on prediction markets. “There’s a real, real problem here,” he says.
entries.content:
Ben McKenzie promised his wife that he was through with being an activist; that he’d go back to the acting gigs that had made him famous. At the end of his documentary taking on the cryptocurrency industry, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money,” the former star of The O.C. and Gotham turned to his spouse and fellow actor Morena Baccarin and swore he was done.

Turns out, that scene might need an edit. McKenzie is launching a new nonprofit, The Public Trust and Transparency Project, that not only continues his battle with the crypto business but widens it to fight prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi.

McKenzie tells WIRED he’s worried about “the gamification of the economy and the notion that we're turning everything into gambling—both investments, in the form of cryptocurrencies, and “prediction markets,” which look an awful lot like online casinos.”

“The more gambling gets into our culture, the more people feel like it's somehow a good idea to view these things as legitimate investment strategies,” he says. The prediction markets reject the comparison (although 80 percent of Kalshi’s trades came from sports in September, according to Bloomberg). McKenzie rejects the rejection: “I mean, if your investment strategy is, ‘I'm going to gamble on the Spurs-Knicks,’ like, come on! So there's a real, real problem here.”

John Reed Stark, who spent 18 years in the Securities and Exchange Commission’s enforcement division, will serve as an adviser to the Project. American Kleptocracy author Casey Michel and Tonantzin Carmona, who runs economic policy for the left-of-center Century Foundation, will sit on the board.

The group is coming together at a time when regulators and law enforcement officials at every level are looking to rein in prediction markets. Federal regulators have launched new probes into both major prediction markets. The GOP-led House Oversight Committee recently released its investigation into US troops and government insiders trading on insider knowledge on Polymarket and Kalshi. The Senate just passed a bill prohibiting prediction markets for military operations and assassinations. Executives at the markets know they’re in for a rough few months; Kalshi even launched an ad campaign, starring Martha Stewart, reminding its users not to trade on confidential information.

But insider trading is only one concern among many. There’s also the problem you find in old-school gambling houses too: The vast majority of people who use the markets lose their money. A recent Wall Street Journal report shows that .01 percent of accounts take in two-thirds of all of the profits on Polymarket. On Kalshi, unprofitable accounts outpace profitable ones by almost three to one.

Then there’s the corruption angle, which McKenzie says is going to be front-and-center for the Project, especially with it featuring as a top issue in the recent midterm elections. Donald Trump Jr. was, until recently, a paid adviser to Kalshi. Trump Jr.’s venture firm, 1789 Capital, made its latest and biggest in a series of investments in Polymarket over the summer; months earlier, the Trump Justice Department sued the state of Minnesota when it tried to ban the prediction markets in the state. (At a recent conference, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called Trump Jr.’s involvement “heavily overblown. We have all types of investors.”)

Prediction markets have been around for hundreds of years, as a forthcoming book on the subject notes. American academics have been turning to them as teaching tools since the late ’80s. Their advocates note that they can be an effective way to hedge against risk, and a form of trading on sports that’s far more consumer-friendly than the online gambling houses. “I accept that there may be some utility,” McKenzie notes. “I'm not saying these things should not exist. I'm just saying they need to be properly regulated.”

McKenzie’s plan will be to push Congress in that direction, sort of the inverse of how the former actor lobbied publicly and privately against the “Clarity Act,” which would’ve brought cryptocurrencies into the financial mainstream. (The bill was rejected in September.)

That pressure is only bound to increase when Democrats take control of Congress next year. “In the bold new world starting [on the] first Monday in January,” Representative Frank Lucas, an Oklahoma Republican, told Politico, “nobody’s untouchable anymore.”

entries.title: Best Early Black Friday AirPods Deals (2026)
entries.summary: Black Friday is just days away, but AirPods discounts are dropping early.
entries.content:
Black Friday is just a few days away, but early Black Friday deals on some of our favorite tech have already rolled in, including Apple’s AirPods. Both the flagship AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2 are on sale, knocking up to $130 off their regular prices. Whether you want pocketable earbuds for everyday use, premium noise-canceling headphones, or seamless Apple integration, these are some of the best prices I've seen recently. I don't expect these prices to go back up until after Black Friday, but with tech getting more expensive, I wouldn't wait too long if you've been planning to upgrade.

Want more deals? Check out our guide to the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Amazon, the Best Early Black Friday TV Deals, and Black Friday Deals at Home Depot.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Apple AirPods Pro 3 for $149 ($100 Off)

The flagship AirPods Pro 3 are Apple’s best AirPods yet. Upgrades include stronger noise-canceling, a new acoustic architecture for deeper bass, and redesigned ear tips for a more secure fit. The ear tips also keep my AirPods from slipping during longer runs and sweatier workouts. New tools include a built-in heart rate sensor for fitness tracking, live translation, and a camera remote to snap photos or videos on your iPhone. These earbuds are also the first AirPods to be IP57 rated against dust, sweat, and rain.

Right now, they are 40 percent off at Amazon, Best Buy, Target, and Walmart. This is the lowest price I’ve ever seen them drop to, and there’s no telling if these discounts will change once Black Friday is here. In other words, I’d grab a pair now if they’re on your wish list.

Apple AirPods Max 2 for $419 ($130 Off)

The AirPods Max 2’s newer H2 chip improves active noise cancellation and transparency mode and enables a suite of intelligent features, including conversation awareness, live translation, and improved Siri interactions. The AirPods Max 2 are designed with a new high-dynamic-range amplifier for deeper bass, more natural vocals, and cleaner highs. The ear cuffs, while plush and comfortable for longer listening sessions, do trap some heat, but I have yet to find a pair of over-ear headphones that don’t.

At $549, the AirPods Max 2 can be a tough sell, especially with so many excellent, more affordable alternatives on the market. But at $130 off, they’re a lot easier to justify, especially if you want the seamless integration that comes with Apple’s ecosystem.

entries.title: ‘GTA 6’ Is a Birder’s Paradise
entries.summary: Here’s what it’s like to grab a pair of binoculars and go in search of the 62 species of birds that populate the game.
entries.content:
Grand Theft Auto VI has received near-universal acclaim and could be the highest-grossing entertainment launch in history. But it holds a more esoteric honor: It might be the most accurately rendered depiction of Florida’s bird life to appear in a video game.

Rockstar Games has filled the latest GTA installation with over 170 animal species that players can tally in their logbook. At the same time, there’s been an explosion of interest in birdwatching, especially among young people, since the last GTA came out 13 years ago. While many players have gotten busy stealing jets and going to strip clubs, birders and streamers are doing “ornithologist runs” to see as many bird species as they can.

I myself am not a gamer, but I’m an avid birder based in New York City who’s familiar with a few indie birdwatching games like Alba and Flock Around, and I have done a bit of birding in Florida—which GTA VI is modeled after, with Vice City being a stand-in for Miami. So I was hungry to get my hands on GTA VI and see the birds for myself. Were the details of GTA VI’s avian NPCs as lifelike as its human ones? (Full disclosure that a friend of mine worked on the game, though not the birds specifically.)

You receive a pair of binoculars with the first mission, and most of the map is open to explore once the intro is over, so you can begin your birding adventures immediately. I left the house and walked around town, trying to get a sense of the neighborhood and searching for places I knew I’d find wildlife, as I would in real life. It turns out you don’t have to look hard. Birds are everywhere in GTA VI—brown pelicans soared overhead, a flock of house sparrows alighted onto a telephone wire, and a blue jay stared down at me as I rounded a corner.

I zeroed in on a gull perched atop a building and noticed its partial black hood of feathers, an adult laughing gull. In a sign of how committed Rockstar is to accurately portraying the real world, I walked further and noticed a bird with the same shape, but it was grayer and light on the black feathers, an immature laughing gull.

This is GTA VI, and all means of improving your birding experience are at your disposal—legal or not. With that in mind, I headed toward the water and performed my first act of theft, jacking a kayak so I could inspect the mangroves and sandy islands in the bay. While motorboats were available, I opted for human-powered to avoid scaring the birds.

The sky was filled with iconic South Florida birds like white ibises, magnificent frigate birds, and osprey. I shouted excitedly on spotting a flock of Caspian terns loafing on a small islet’s shore, then eyed a spotted sandpiper. The latter didn’t have its real-world analogue’s “twerking” strut (a big missed opportunity for a GTA game), but its physical appearance was accurate. I beached my kayak and went ashore, where I eyed a pair of great blue herons and then scared a tricolored heron from a shrub as I sprinted away from a crocodile I nearly stepped on.

I was impressed by the game developer’s commitment to accurately rendering South Florida’s coastal mangrove habitats, which provide shelter for an abundance of fish, food for birds, and serve as a habitat for the threatened American crocodile. However, they only host so much avian diversity.

To see more species, I drove north through the various habitats in and around the fictional city of Leonida and stopped to scan the skies. I spotted American robins, northern mockingbirds, and “New World orioles,” the game’s analog to the Baltimore oriole, which I assumed is named as such because Baltimore is not part of the Grand Theft Auto universe. Downtown Vice City featured non-native peacocks and rock pigeons—the latter of which were introduced to North America in the 1600s. When I arrived at the pine-covered areas north of the city, I began seeing red-cockaded woodpeckers and scrub jays, an analog to the rare Florida scrub-jay that similarly inhabits sand pine areas north of Miami and is endemic to the state of Florida.

Birders who’ve been to Florida will find Leonida’s abundance and distribution of wildlife familiar. As in meatspace, pelicans and ibises are constantly flying overhead, and wading birds fill every body of water. Birds are properly segregated into their habitats, with songbirds and city birds in built-up areas, shorebirds and long-legged wading birds in wetlands. In both the game and real life, despite intensive human development, birds still attempt to survive where they can.

The birds’ behaviors are also accurate beyond standing and flying. As I was trying to study my first bald eagle, a pair of crows flew over to chase it, a behavior regularly seen in the wild to scare large raptors away. Monk parakeets preened while perching on a wire, and a juvenile northern mockingbird did its characteristic wing flicking. Meanwhile, GTA VI’s great blue herons always seem to be having sex, not something I’ve noticed in real life but a silly detail nonetheless.

Frankly, the whole experience of driving around while distractedly watching telephone wires and roadsides or pulling over to check every little water body is itself the most accurate representation of the Florida birding experience.

My other birding friends who have played the game concurred. “The first thing I thought was how closely this resembles birding in Florida,” says accomplished bird author Nick Lund, who has done extensive birdwatching in Red Dead Redemption II, another game where avian life is a big part of gameplay, and is currently doing a GTA VI birding speed run. He’s noticed other in-game birding Easter eggs—for example, he’s encountered spot-breasted orioles, a Central American species introduced to southeastern Florida that birdwatchers specifically target when visiting Miami.

While impressive in its fidelity to real life, GTA VI’s avian depictions aren’t 100 percent accurate. I found the flight styles and silhouettes of many birds to be a little off, while some renditions missed the mark—the abundant crows all feel too long and pale. While walking around Jason’s neighborhood, Lund and I both noticed the apparent song of the bananaquit, a Caribbean species that rarely appears in the US. The game is also filled with whooping cranes, one of the rarest birds in the US. They’re also mostly gone from Florida after an unsuccessful reintroduction effort, where sandhill cranes are much more common. (Maybe the makers of GTA VI are telling real-world conservationists to try harder next time.) Lund flagged that the roseate spoonbill seems to make the call of the willow ptarmigan—a detail he also noticed in RDR II. And somehow I’ve yet to spot a bird in a tree, but this may be a skill issue.

Ultimately, GTA VI isn’t a birdwatching game, and does lag behind the real world and birdwatching-specific games in terms of avian content. Sixty-two species might sound like a lot, but birders in Miami-Dade County have spotted more than 240 species in November 2026 alone, and one real-life birder in Miami spotted 61 species in a two-hour stint on the day of the game’s release.

There’s a certain magic and unpredictability to birdwatching that the game doesn’t nail—finding a migratory warbler in a hotel parking lot, catching an egret hunting anoles in a topiary, or spotting an out-of-place vagrant bird are all real-life thrills the game can’t fully capture. Of course, GTA VI also has an actual plot and storyline that I surmise might be slightly more important to its developers and the majority of the gaming public than solely building the world’s most accurate Florida birding simulator.

Still, GTA VI’s animal observation mechanics have continued to delight after 12 hours of play. Birding is certainly an auxiliary part of the game, rather than its core thrust—but if you’re a birder wondering whether to play the game just for its birds, I think you’ll still have plenty of fun.

entries.title: Now There’s a GLP-1 in Chocolate Form
entries.summary: A telehealth clinic is offering orforglipron, the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s prescription weight-loss pill Foundayo, in edible chocolate squares. Lilly is not amused.
entries.content:
First came GLP-1 injections, then GLP-1 pills. Now there’s GLP-1 chocolate. That’s right, a GLP-1 drug in chocolate.

To be clear, this isn’t a new medication rubber-stamped by the Food and Drug Administration. It’s a copycat product offered by telehealth outfit Journi Health, and it’s aptly called Melt. The chocolate morsels, which are taken once daily, contain orforglipron, the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s prescription weight-loss pill Foundayo. (Eli Lilly also makes the GLP-1 injectable medications Mounjaro and Zepbound.)

As GLP-1 shots exploded in popularity, Lilly and Novo Nordisk, which makes Ozempic and Wegovy, knew they could appeal to even more patients if they put their drugs in pill form.

“One of the bigger barriers to adoption has been that some patients just don't want to take an injection,” Ken Custer, executive vice president of Eli Lilly, previously told WIRED. Foundayo was approved in April, while a pill version of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy won approval in December 2025.

And here’s where Journi Health’s pitch comes in. Founder Luna Yu says Melt is for people who have difficulty with injections or swallowing pills, including those who are new to GLP-1s as well as those already taking one who are looking to maintain their current weight. “Lastly, it's for the microdosers who are looking for the longevity benefits,” she says. (For the record, taking any GLP-1 medication below the lowest FDA-approved or standard therapeutic dose has not been tested or proven effective in human trials.)

Yu isn’t a doctor, but Melt does require a prescription from one. Would-be patients go through a virtual medical evaluation where a licensed clinician reviews their health history, determines if Melt is a good fit, and sets the dose. It costs $189 for a monthly subscription of 24 individually wrapped squares of chocolate, which includes physician review. (Foundayo’s list price is $649 for a 30-day supply, but with insurance it could be much lower.)

Melt is considered a compounded drug, essentially a custom mix made for a patient by a pharmacy using FDA-approved ingredients but with a formulation that is not itself FDA approved. The FDA allows pharmacies to compound medications when there’s a patient need—for instance, if a patient is allergic to a dye or ingredient in a medication or needs a smaller dose because of their weight—or when the brand-name version is in shortage.

When injectable GLP-1s were in shortage from 2022 through early 2025, compounding pharmacies were allowed to make their own versions for patients, leading to a booming online market. Telehealth companies sold their versions for a fraction of the price of the name-brand medications, making them a more affordable option for people without insurance coverage for GLP-1s.

Now that commercial GLP-1s are no longer in shortage, the FDA says pharmacies cannot routinely compound what are “essentially copies” en masse, though there are some exceptions for documented, patient-specific medical needs.

FDA has expressed particular concerns with unapproved GLP-1 drugs and has cracked down on virtual clinics selling them. Eli Lilly has filed multiple lawsuits against companies selling them, but the drugs still remain available online.

When asked about Journi’s Melt, a spokesperson for Eli Lilly told WIRED, “Foundayo is an FDA-approved oral orforglipron medicine, which was developed through years of innovative science and backed by robust clinical trials. An unstudied knockoff that uses chocolate for purported weight loss treats a serious health need as a marketing gimmick. Regulators and law enforcement must take decisive action against knockoff products being marketed to unsuspecting consumers.”

Yu says Journi Health is able to offer Melt because it’s not an exact copy of the original. “It's really in a novel form factor whereby it allows the patient to have a different experience.” Plus, she says, an edible formulation meets a need for patients who have trouble with injections or swallowing pills.

“We've spoken with patients who've discontinued treatment because of these barriers,” she says. “They deserve alternatives worth exploring.”

Whether the FDA will find this convincing remains to be determined. For now, though, all that stands between patients and the “novel form factor” is a few clicks.
